rich_summary: After a year of flawless service to a visiting ascetic, the maiden Pritha (Kunti) earns his deep satisfaction. When she refuses personal boons out of humility, the sage instead grants her a powerful Atharvan mantra that can summon any celestial being and compel that deity to obey her. Curious about its power, the young and unmarried Kunti later tests it at dawn by invoking Surya, the Sun god. Surya appears in radiant form, divided so that the sun continues shining while his divine presence stands before her. Alarmed, Kunti asks him to return, admitting she called him only out of curiosity. Surya refuses to leave without purpose, insisting she accept a son from him and threatening a curse if she refuses. The scene captures the dangerous power of divine gifts and sets in motion the fateful conception of Karna, one of the epic’s most tragic heroes.

highlight_spans.why: Kunti’s year of flawless service culminates in the sage’s offer of extraordinary boons, establishing her virtue and the circumstances that lead to the gift of the mantra.
The sage explains the mantra’s astonishing power: any celestial invoked must appear and submit to the caller’s will.
Kunti’s curiosity leads her to test the mantra and invoke Surya at sunrise, a pivotal act that triggers the coming tragedy.
Kunti’s fearful plea for Surya to depart shows her shame and vulnerability as an unmarried girl suddenly confronted with a god.
Surya pressures Kunti, threatening curses if she refuses him, intensifying the moral and emotional conflict of the moment.

top_scenes.scene_text: At dawn in her chamber, young Kunti gazes at the rising sun as the radiant god Surya manifests before her in golden armor and earrings, illuminating the room with divine light.
Surya stands before the frightened maiden while, in the sky above, the gathered celestials watch from the firmament as witnesses to the tense encounter.
The ascetic bestows the secret mantra upon Kunti in the royal court while King Kuntibhoja looks on in reverent amazement.
